items.title: Dune: Awakening On PS5 Is Making Me Break My Rule Against Playing Survival Games
items.author: Zack Zwiezen

items.text:
At some point in recent years, I realized I didn’t enjoy survival crafting games, aka tree punchers. At first, the thrill of exploring a new world and building a little fort in the woods was fun, but quickly—usually within the first few hours—I’d realize the treadmill I was on, and I would stop playing. Rarely did the moment-to-moment gameplay win me over and keep me slogging through the grind. So I’m very surprised that I’ve spent well over a dozen hours playing MMO survival RPG Dune: Awakening on PS5 and intend to play a lot more.

Released last year on PC, Dune: Awakening recently leaped to PS5 and Xbox as part of a large update that also added a ton of gameplay options to the third-person sci-fi survival game, as well as new story content, plenty of quality-of-life improvements, a full single-player mode, and the ability to completely avoid PvP if you so desire. I played a little bit of the game back at launch on PC, but it wasn’t until the last week that I finally sat down and got lost in the sands of Arrakis.

The first thing I was happy to discover is that Dune: Awakening runs great on PS5 and feels perfectly at home on a controller. Inventory management, base building, combat, and exploration (both on foot and via vehicle) feel good. I never missed having a mouse in my hand. If anything, playing Dune with a PS5 gamepad on my big TV made it feel more like an action-adventure game than some Steam-only survival-crafter, which likely helped me not bounce off it as hard.

I created a character and played through the opening hours of Dune: Awakening via its new single-player mode, which worked flawlessly and delivered an experience that didn’t feel like a stripped-down MMO survival game. But eventually, as I was completing quests and leveling up my lone soldier, trying to survive the harsh deserts of Arrakis by harvesting blood and dew water, my brother hopped on and wanted to play together. To do this, I had to create a new character, as single-player characters can’t hop to multiplayer servers. A bit annoying, but thankfully after you’ve gone through the tutorial and opening section of the game, you can just skip it when creating a new character. This is a wonderful feature.

Together, my brother and I built up a ramshackle little hut in the desert and began harvesting materials and killing random bandits for resources. (And blood.) And this is where I think Dune: Awakening wins me over compared to so many other survival crafting games.

Harvesting stuff is fun. You scan rocks and other objects and then use a laser to cut across a highlighted spot. The thing pops apart, and you automatically get the resources. It’s not annoying, time-consuming, or tedious.

Meanwhile, combat is actually pretty good, too. No, Dune: Awakening can’t compete with the best third-person shooters or action games out there, but combat feels snappy, dangerous, and responsive. Ducking in and out of cover during firefights or using my knife to pop an enemy’s holo-shield never made me feel like I was just watching an animation play out, which the combat in a lot of MMOs does. Nor does it feel clunky or janky, like in a lot of survival games. Instead. I actually enjoy fighting enemies in Dune: Awakening, to the point that I sometimes seek out combat just to hunt down some bandits while killing time.

Playing with someone definitely made Dune: Awakening even more enjoyable. And like the game’s performance on console, I was impressed by how rock-solid my online sessions have been, with almost no lag or weird issues. It just works, and that’s nice in 2026.

I’m not a Dune sicko at all. I’ve not seen any of the new movies, though I plan on watching all three later this year. I’ve only read the first book, and that was back when I was in middle school. Yet I’ve always appreciated the universe and tone of Dune, and I think the game mostly nails those vibes. The planet of Arrakis feels deadly and ancient. The massive ships hovering above feel impossible and oppressive. And there’s a real sense that, especially early on, you are a small part of something much, much larger. Something you don’t really understand. I expect Dune lovers will have a great time picking up on all the references and Easter eggs that I imagine are stuffed in Dune: Awakening; personally, I’m just having a blast surviving in this world.

That’s not to say you can’t also have some silly fun in Dune: Awakening’s digital Arrakis.

At the tail end of one late-night Dune session, my brother and I wanted to screw around with the large desert worm that stalks the sands of Dune: Awakening. You have to be careful when crossing open sand, or you can be gobbled up by this big bastard and lose everything you’re carrying forever. But after a couple of nights of dodging the worm and barely escaping with our lives, curiosity got the better of us. We both wanted to poke at the beast.

So my brother removed all his gear and clothing and ran out into the sandy dunes outside our base to attract the worm. At that point, Dune: Awakening became an episode of Jackass, and after toying around with the worm, my brother’s luck ran out, and he was consumed by the big creature in a moment I wish I had captured a screenshot of, but I was laughing too hard to do so.

So yeah, I’m having a great time with Dune: Awakening. I have no idea if the endgame is good or bad. I don’t know if there’s some negative meta change that people are mad about. I don’t really care, to be honest. I’m having a good time both solo and with my brother in Dune: Awakening. I can’t believe it. I found a survival crafting game in 2026 that I don’t hate. Wild stuff.

items.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered Just Broke A Steam Record As People Rush Back To Play A New And Improved Version Of One Of The Best RPGs Ever
items.author: Ethan Gach

items.text:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is out today and propelling the 11-year-old open-world RPG back up the Steam charts. In fact, the game just broke a new concurrent player record. And for good reason, too. The remaster, a free upgrade that improves visuals and tweaks gameplay, really does feel worth returning for.

The Witcher 3 peaked at under 100,000 concurrent players back when it first released on Steam. Now it’s over 120,000 and still rising. Valve’s storefront wasn’t nearly as popular then as it is today, especially in markets like China. But major sales and updates have seen the numbers spike in more recent years as well, though nothing like today’s peak in popularity. Even the 2023 next-gen update for consoles, which also came to PC, didn’t come close.

It no doubt helps that The Witcher 3 is currently on sale for 50 percent off, and the remastered update is free to everyone who already owns the game, providing the perfect reason to dip back into one of the best fantasy RPGs ever made. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered includes not just gameplay changes and visual improvements, but entirely overhauled UI systems and new features like a photo mode that lets you changes the weather and time of day on demand.

The full list of patch notes is on CD Projekt Red’s website and is quite long. There are over 70 individual tweaks and fixes laid out, as well as platform-specific updates like updated graphics modes on PS5 and in-menu mouse controls on Switch. There are also spec sheets for running the game at ultra settings on PC, with users now needing a GeForce RTX 5080 and 24GB of RAM to max out the visual detail and performance. Unfortunately, there are also reports of players with AMD graphics cards running into trouble due to missing driver support in the new update.

Switch 2 owners, however, appear to be in for a rare treat. The Witcher 3 was one of the more ambitious ports for the original Switch and one that arguably didn’t really pan out. It ran, but with tons of compromises that made it hard to recommend, even for people who had no other way of playing it. The experience on Switch 2, a free upgrade for owners of the last-gen version, appears to be making good on the promise of the original port, and offering a quality experience in line with what players got in the Cyberpunk 2077 port last year. I haven’t had a chance to try it yet, but those who have report decent results that are at least above the base-level experience on PS4 and Xbox One.

In fact, there are so many upgrades floating around in the latest version of The Witcher 3 that some fans were worried that its unofficial mascot had been buffed out of existence. A low-poly pigeon was photographed and went viral back in 2023. The meme now lives in Witcher fans’ hearts alongside pictures of Geralt in a bathtub. When one player took a photo of a pigeon standing on the ground from the remaster that showed it with a new level of detail, players initially freaked out, worried that CD Projekt Red had murdered low-poly.

I did a bit of digging myself, however, and confirmed that she remains intact. The models for pigeons when they are flying in the air are different from those of them standing around. CD Projekt Red confirmed to me that no changes were made to the airborne asset, though the one on the ground did get some extra polish. “The flying low-poly pigeon is there, and will remain there so we don’t upset too many people externally OR internally!” a spokesperson confirmed to Kotaku.

I’ve spent several days with the remaster and will try to have some more in-depth impressions soon. Generally though, it’s quite good, even if I’m not sold on all of the visual changes. Mostly, I’m just grateful to have another good reason to go back and replay a masterpiece. It’s wild how well it still holds up.

https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/ss_c6d0b7eee8d40b55d33621fcd700151f3325b501.1920x1080.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/witchers-song-past-3.jpg

The Witcher 3 peaked at under 100,000 concurrent players back when it first released on Steam. Now it’s over 120,000 and still rising. Valve’s storefront wasn’t nearly as popular then as it is today, especially in markets like China. But major sales and updates have seen the numbers spike in more recent years as well, though nothing like today’s peak in popularity. Even the 2023 next-gen update for consoles, which also came to PC, didn’t come close.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/witcher-3-blurr.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/ss_8ad5c9ab448b43bcc65350898e50ddefcb5c9ad4.1920x1080-1.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/we-playground.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/Witcher-3-steam-chart.jpg

It no doubt helps that The Witcher 3 is currently on sale for 50 percent off, and the remastered update is free to everyone who already owns the game, providing the perfect reason to dip back into one of the best fantasy RPGs ever made. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered includes not just gameplay changes and visual improvements, but entirely overhauled UI systems and new features like a photo mode that lets you changes the weather and time of day on demand.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/xenogears.jpg

The full list of patch notes is on CD Projekt Red’s website and is quite long. There are over 70 individual tweaks and fixes laid out, as well as platform-specific updates like updated graphics modes on PS5 and in-menu mouse controls on Switch. There are also spec sheets for running the game at ultra settings on PC, with users now needing a GeForce RTX 5080 and 24GB of RAM to max out the visual detail and performance. Unfortunately, there are also reports of players with AMD graphics cards running into trouble due to missing driver support in the new update.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/FFVII_Revelation_June_Screenshots_16.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2024/11/118b4825e679e993bfabee1b560ccd65-160x160.jpg
blocks.c: A PS5 Pro appears in front of a multi-color background.

blocks.x: https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/witchers-song-past-3-160x160.jpg

Switch 2 owners, however, appear to be in for a rare treat. The Witcher 3 was one of the more ambitious ports for the original Switch and one that arguably didn’t really pan out. It ran, but with tons of compromises that made it hard to recommend, even for people who had no other way of playing it. The experience on Switch 2, a free upgrade for owners of the last-gen version, appears to be making good on the promise of the original port, and offering a quality experience in line with what players got in the Cyberpunk 2077 port last year. I haven’t had a chance to try it yet, but those who have report decent results that are at least above the base-level experience on PS4 and Xbox One.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2025/05/524bea00bf57b888c62fb04624c1f9ae-160x160.jpg
blocks.c: A man and woman sit in a bed.

blocks.x: In fact, there are so many upgrades floating around in the latest version of The Witcher 3 that some fans were worried that its unofficial mascot had been buffed out of existence. A low-poly pigeon was photographed and went viral back in 2023. The meme now lives in Witcher fans’ hearts alongside pictures of Geralt in a bathtub. When one player took a photo of a pigeon standing on the ground from the remaster that showed it with a new level of detail, players initially freaked out, worried that CD Projekt Red had murdered low-poly.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/xbox-disc-stack-160x160.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/Dune-ps5-2-160x160.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/monster-hunter-wilds-160x160.jpg

I did a bit of digging myself, however, and confirmed that she remains intact. The models for pigeons when they are flying in the air are different from those of them standing around. CD Projekt Red confirmed to me that no changes were made to the airborne asset, though the one on the ground did get some extra polish. “The flying low-poly pigeon is there, and will remain there so we don’t upset too many people externally OR internally!” a spokesperson confirmed to Kotaku.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/witcher-3-blurr-160x160.jpg

I’ve spent several days with the remaster and will try to have some more in-depth impressions soon. Generally though, it’s quite good, even if I’m not sold on all of the visual changes. Mostly, I’m just grateful to have another good reason to go back and replay a masterpiece. It’s wild how well it still holds up.

items.title: Why so many Steam games have weirdly similar (and forgettable) names
items.author: Samuel Roberts
items.summary: Duskfade. DUST: Origins. Dust Front RTS. Duskbloods. Dungeons of Dusk. These are all games that will be released in a 12-month period. I know the differences
items.text:
Duskfade. DUST: Origins. Dust Front RTS. Duskbloods. Dungeons of Dusk. These are all games that will be released in a 12-month period. I know the differences between them, but I'm convinced that no normal person would be able to remember all of these titles.

Dungeons of Dusk gets a pass, because it's a spin-off of a rad FPS that led the boomer shooter revival movement. That's easy enough to remember. Duskbloods is the new FromSoftware game, so there's no chance anyone will forget that.

But, I will pick on DUST: Origins and Duskfade. Want to know the origins of dust? That stuff gathering on your monitor and shelves? Dead skin (and other debris). That title stirs nothing within me, even though the game has some solid development pedigree behind it.

Duskfade is a perfectly pleasant 3D platformer with Kingdom Hearts-style combat that came out a couple of months ago. Once I've finished typing this paragraph, however, it will once again erase itself from my memory, because there's nothing evocative about the name.

So many video game names are either daft, interchangeable, or confusing. I got thinking about this because of a great thread by Hannah Flynn, communications director at Failbetter and a games marketing consultant. She's previously worked for brands like Penguin Books and Tate in the UK.

"Put aside what you think a game name should sound like," the advice reads. "There are thousands upon thousands of games on Steam now. Not all of them are named well, and there are weird trends which actually make your name less effective. Start with your game!"

That is surely the number one problem with most game names: people look at other games' names and try to pick something that sounds a bit like them. The result is often a flavourless mush that struggles to stay in the memory. To an outsider not already well-versed in the games marketplace, these often sound ridiculous.

The dust/dusk-relevant nugget I particularly like in Flynn's thread said to watch out for "filler" words like:

- "fall of" (11,527 results on Steam)
- "echoes of" (2,750 results on Steam)
- "shadow of" (8,243 results on Steam)

No offence to the developers of DUST: Origins, but 'origins' is absolutely of those words.

"There isn't a universal formula [for a good game name]," Flynn summarises. "But I like to think that a good name reflects the spirit of the game, and doesn't go out of its way to be un-memorable." She offers plenty of examples: Hades, Clickolding, Dave the Diver, Failbetter's own Sunless Skies.

This all resonated with me because I've been writing about games for 19 years, and I've seen a lot of bad game names in that time. A former colleague of mine used to bring up the games Violence Fight and Faster than Speed as being classically terrible titles for games—but those names are actually funny, whereas I think bland or generic names are much more annoying and widespread. In the Xbox 360 era where everyone wanted their version of Call of Duty or Gears of War, these proliferated.

Name that game

Hades is a great name for a game, let's face it. (Image credit: Supergiant)I decided to ask Flynn a bit more about the hypotheses shared in her thread, hoping to dig into the unhinged thought process behind every game name that ends with 'unleashed' or 'chronicles'. "I've thought about this more than is reasonable," Flynn says.

"I've been making indie games at Failbetter Games for 12 years, and have also reviewed hundreds of Steam store pages for other teams. I've developed this interest in game naming out of a professional need, but also because I'm getting older and my memory is getting worse, and I'd like to be able to recall the names of games I want to play."

I empathise with Flynn's point on age. One test is whether you can still remember what a game is called 10 minutes after you saw it announced in one of Geoff Keighley's showcases. Sorry *checks notes* TARAE: The Unbound, but even though I watched that trailer just one month ago at Opening Night Live, my memory had flushed that one away before the livestream was even over. A bad game name can trip a developer at the starting line.

TARAE looks pretty neat – it just didn't strike me as a great name for a game. (Image credit: Krafton)When developers look to other games to name theirs, "The possibility space spirals in on itself, and suddenly everything's called Rise of the Bonelord: Origins of Dust," she says.

"It's a fragment of a broader insularity in the industry. You can tell when games are only inspired by other games. I'm a big believer in looking to history, art, science, performance, nature, comics and pretty much everything else as inspirations for both making games, and naming them."

The reason a decent name matters, of course, is that we've got more of the things to choose from than ever. It's another way to make your game visible in the morass.

"Steam is a very densely populated platform these days," Flynn says. "To catch people's interest you only really have the name of your game and the capsule art, and there's only so much they can do. It's really an artform to create both and make them work well together in a way that stands out."

I asked GameDiscoverCo founder Simon Carless about this topic, who offers a slightly different take. "I think it's important that developers pick a name that's not too long and convoluted, and won't be immediately confused with another game. (The Outer Wilds vs. The Outer Worlds being the most famous of those name clashes.)

"Beyond that—I actually think that naming isn't that important, since most people buy a game based on video footage, someone else playing it, or a recommendation. And we've seen in music and elsewhere that weird names are in no way a blocker to becoming successful." Carless cites Steely Dan and Bananarama as examples.

Form vs function

Big Walk: they called it what you do in the game. (Image credit: Panic)So what defines a good name? "A good name sells the game's vibe," Flynn says. "The feel of how it'll play. There are loads of ways to be successful at this. It could come from a well-known phrase, an idiom, a place name, an artefact, a character's name, or just a concept that reflects the game's theme." Flynn cites a workbook called Don't Call it That, which has helped shape how she thinks about this.

"Finding the right name should feel like a jigsaw piece slotting into place, not that you've completed a 50-step escape room. Big Walk is about having a big walk. If you can, let the game name itself."

This got me thinking about whether the titles of my favourite indie games from the past few years were able to capture their essence. A few certainly did. Ball x Pit? That's a perfect name for that game. Dispatch? The word by itself isn't that evocative, but that does describe the basic act of what you do in the game, and it's simple enough to be memorable. Mouthwashing? That's a cleverly subversive name because it asks the question 'why is it called that?', which the game does pay off.

I think Carless' band analogy is apt—a name can seem clever in retrospect because it has already become iconic. Balatro is a good example of that to me. If LocalThunk's game had 10 reviews on Steam and was completely ignored, I'd probably call that a bad name. Few normal people, after all, would know that Balatro means 'jester' or 'clown' in Latin.

Flynn, though, points out that Balatro is actually a good game name by a few different criteria. "Balatro is a great case study. It's another word for Joker, which gets the seal of approval because it's historical and specific to the game. It's an alt-joker name for an alt-joker game. On the other hand its definition is comparatively little-known, even now, so it does have a slight whiff of thesaurus-digging.

"But! It's a jolly word, fun to say, easy to spell. It also comes from an established tradition. Puzzle-y games can get away with single-word names because of related media like board games (Ludo, Cluedo, Catan, Boggle) and traditional puzzle formats (Sokoban, Sudoku, Rubix). The fact that Balatro is called Balatro places it confidently in that tradition, versus calling it something like Crazy Jokers: Number Go Up, which overexplains the point and ultimately undersells the game to the kind of person who'd be into Balatro."

Flynn points out, too, that the name is so catchy that 'Balatro-likes' is now a widely used term for a whole range of roguelikes. Crazy Jokers-likes doesn't quite have the same ring.

"I think the name of a game can be the difference between someone remembering your game and having it disappear into the ether," says game trailer expert Derek Lieu. "Even if you ignore the fact a very generic name is less likely to show up at the top of search results, a title which sticks is just one more thing that can help it stand out."

Lieu praises SUPERHOT and Unpacking as elegant and memorable titles.

"'A Little to the Left' I think is a brilliant title because it's charming, has nice alliteration, and communicates the game's concept," Lieu adds. "'Tiny Glade' is great because it includes both scope and setting. 'Tokyo Jungle' I love because it's two words which don't belong together and I can't help but be intrigued."

The colon police

(Image credit: Failbetter Games)Concise game names are key, then, but many developers have succumbed to the temptation of throwing in some fancy punctuation and a rubbish subtitle.

"Game names with colons are for series, editions, and DLC," reads Flynn's thread on titles. "Don't give people two names to remember." Confidence is key to avoiding this.

"I think for indie teams, they're afraid of choosing one name and sticking with it," Flynn says about the temptation to dabble with Game: Subtitle naming conventions. "Usually, either side of the colon could work as a name on its own, but uncertainty wins out and they end up diluting their impact. In the end all they're doing is asking players to remember two names instead of one."

It's worth pointing out, too, that few of Flynn's rules are absolute, and that extends to colons. "There are times when you can use a colon without displeasing me, the colon police." A sequel with a returning main character, DLC, ultimate editions—Flynn says those all make sense.

Sometimes a subtitle can also be descriptive, which is useful to the player on a platform like Steam. "I love the name Iron Nest: Heavy Turret Simulator. The subtitle is in the game's name on Steam, so it clarifies what you're doing, but the key art just has this really impactful Iron Nest naming."

Failbetter's next game is called Mandrake—the result of lots of collaborative longlisting, Flynn says. As well as encapsulating horticultural and sorcerer-type themes, it's the name of the game's main character.

Carless says that there are some cases where a descriptive but unflashy game name only does the developer a favour in finding the right audience. "There are a small amount of cases when you can actually use SEO in the name of your game, e.g. if it's a farming game and you can stick 'farming' in there. But in general that's not possible. And... I don't think generic names are always bad if they have the right connotations. For example, if you make a job simulator game, I'm a fan of putting the word 'Simulator' in there. It anchors it…"

There's no precise formula to a great name, then, just an extensive series of best practices to avoid common mistakes. To turn Carless' band analogy on its head: you know a bad name when you're looking at it (Hoobastank). Tapping into the essence of what your game is, and not getting too preoccupied with what other developers are doing, seems like a sensible starting point.

"I hope that when people name their games, they do at least block out 5-10 possibilities and have a serious discussion about it," Carless says. "The first name you think of shouldn't always be the game name."

items.title: I perished in the flesh pipes of Darktide's Depths of the Damned update, and you will too
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide continues to cling tightly, perhaps even aggressively, to my Steam installations, my occasionally waning interest repeatedly
items.text:
Warhammer 40,000: Darktide continues to cling tightly, perhaps even aggressively, to my Steam installations, my occasionally waning interest repeatedly re-sparked by the addition of akimbo-autopistolling chem fiends or haughty toasterpeople. A live service sucker, it makes me. Today's Depths of the Damned update, the grimdark co-op shooter's biggest since the Skitarii rocked up, continues the trend: it's centered around a massive new mission that's as revolting as it is compelling.

Whereas most Darktide excursions take you through criss-crossing sectors of its impossibly gigantic Hive City, the new Spillway deployment dumps you in the gushing, thus-unexplored hell of Tertium's water treatment facility. It’s a spectacular place, in the sense that it's utterly horrible. Fetid green liquid rushes through its caverns as blasphemous new life sprouts from the moisture, dark moss covering the cages that the complex's former gangster ownership probably didn’t hang for aesthetic reasons. The current residents aren't much friendlier, taking full advantage of the space's long sightlines to pelt you with lasgun fire while their fellow crusty cultists charge into melee range.

The Spillway's guts are even nastier. I'd say they’re covered in daemonic growths, but that would suggest the existence of visible points where the Chaos meat first took root. It would be more accurate to say the growths have become structurally integral to the facility in general, entire rooms covered floor-to-ceiling in the muck. The pipe network, meanwhile, is so thickly coated that it starts resembling a badly diseased intestinal tract; a playable Fantastic Voyage, if Raquel Welch was an Ogryn.

Despite this, and with the caveat that I've only played through the new mission once, it doesn't have the radically different feel of certain other post-launch operation additions. 2024's Rolling Steel was a runaway train caper unlike anything Darktide had tried before, and the Hive Scum update's No Man's Land op successfully swapped metal corridors for muddy trenches in a breathless WW1-inspired rush. Spillway is, at least structurally, a much more conventional oscillation of fierce wave combat and quieter traversal.

Those other two missions, however, were comparatively tight, short-form jaunts. This is a full-length, maybe even bumper-sized new challenge, which does at least try to enact some smaller twists along the way. There's a spot of light memory-puzzling, for example, as you’re shown a particular daub of gang graffiti that will mark the safe-ish path through the mazelike pipes – if you can find it among all the other gang graffiti. items.title: Adult Swim’s “Get Jiro” Serves Up Bloody, Sloppy Culinary Revenge
items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One,
items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

items.title: This week in PC games: new Ace Combat, Transport Fever 3, and a System Shock-alike set on a disco space station
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell

items.text:
Happy this week all! ...Ugh, you are all still here. When I went on holiday last week, I was hoping that I'd return to find that the whole "videogame journalism career" thing was just a fleeting delusion brought on by excess consumption of unripe pears. Perhaps I've actually been a wealthy gentleman gadabout this whole time, free of any need to keep the hellmouth topped up with layoff reports in order to stave off deprivation and disaster.

The one consolation - other than EIC Julian's many encouraging facial expressions and hand gestures – is that people are still making new PC games, and a few of them are actually quite interesting! Here's the latest list of new releases.

Monday 28th September

No, I refuse to believe that my holiday is over. Let's all get the heck down to Camp Whittlewood, a pixelart horror RPG about cub scouts going camping in the deep forest, featuring absolutely no serial killers.

Camp Whittlewood aside, there are precious few holiday-themed games on this list. Instead, we have games like HR: Human Remains. It's about being an office clerk in Hell, after humans lost a war with the demons. Get through your to-do list, or get fed to the Maw (no relation).

Yots is a PS1-ified co-op extraction game in which you repeatedly pillage a procgen city that looks like Silent Hill, assuming Silent Hill existed in the 1930s. I'm pretty sure it did. I don't think they had Pyramid Head technology back then, but they certainly had fog.

Speaking of lumbering metal monsters - where are my 90s Mechwarrior enjoyers? Drop Command is here with a mixture of cockpit combat and overarching 4X elements.

Tuesday 29th September

Nivalis Nights is a cyberpunk restaurant management game and life sim from the makers of Cloudpunk. The views should be pretty lush, whatever you may think of the jobbing element. Alas, my holiday!

Toem 2 is the new toem' up from John Toem, developer of Toem. (Actual studio name: Something We Made. Actual game description: a gentle diorama platformer and photography puzzler.)

Transport Fever 3 is the latest borderline masturbatory infrastructure meddler from Paradox, featuring the shiniest trains you ever did see.

From the makers of Human Fall Flat, here's Tiny Flock, a VR shepherding sim with more seesaws, circus machines and great white sharks than I believe is traditional, in real-life shepherding.

Wednesday 30th September

Radiosol casts you as a mechanical spider exploring a fallen world of attractively dusty and dessicated megastructures. It does use genAI to translate the game into Spanish, Japanese, German, French, and Chinese. I am underlining my own reminder to write/commission a piece on genAI translation in gamedev.

Okko The Exiled is a pretty gorgeous 2D sidescroller about some diminutive fellow with horns and a massive club. Look at him go!

Songs of Glimmerwick is a witch school RPG in which magic and music are closely allied. The developers are promising "hijinks". Don't… tempt me, Frodo!

Crusader Kings 3: By God Alone is the CK3 expansion in which you can run the Vatican and do all kinds of notionally un-Christian things – just ask Julian.

Thursday 1st October

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is an Unreal Engineered revamp of the early noughties musou masher and its Xtreme Legends expandalone. Always had a sneaking fondness for DW games, despite the fact that they often play like lawnmower simulators in which the grass consists of shrieking spear guys.

RetroSpace (pictured) is the immersive sim with Saturday Night Fever vibes in which you, a janitor, try to survive inside a space station that has been yoinked into a blackhole.

There are planes in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Bamco's latest Hot Shots-alike.

Friday 2nd October

What's the weather like there? On-going UK drought notwithstanding, we're edging into the golden season where you still get a few immaculate summer skies, but elegantly merged with the crispness and enchantment of autumn. Argh, having to undertake 'gainful employment' in these conditions is an offence to Nature. Now is the time to be out of doors, cavorting in the leaves, rather than staying inside to play/write about smelly videogames. Although if you have any new releases to recommend, we'd be interested as ever. Have a jolly week.

items.title: The 10 Best Slice-of-Life Books, Ranked
items.author: Luc Haasbroek
items.summary: Not every great book needs an elaborate plot. Slice-of-life literature finds significance in experiences that might otherwise seem ordinary. Sometimes, simply
items.text:
Not every great book needs an elaborate plot. Slice-of-life literature finds significance in experiences that might otherwise seem ordinary. Sometimes, simply watching people work, eat, fall in love, grieve, make mistakes, talk to friends, or quietly wonder whether they've made the right choices can be every bit as compelling as a grand adventure.

Needless to say, this approach is more difficult to pull off, requiring a greater focus on character development and compelling prose. Yet a few writers have more than succeeded, turning seemingly mundane storylines into literary masterpieces. Here are a few of the best of them, ranked.

10
'The Perks of Being a Wallflower' (1999)

Image via MTV Books

"And in that moment, I swear we were infinite." Adolescence can feel simultaneously completely ordinary and overwhelmingly important. Stephen Chbosky captures that contradiction beautifully in both the Perks of Being a Wallflower book and movie (which he also directed). It's a coming-of-age story composed of letters written by Charlie, a shy high-school freshman trying to navigate friendship, romance, family, mental health, and the complicated process of becoming more actively involved in his own life. His circumstances aren't fantastical, but to Charlie, every party, conversation, crush, and song can carry enormous emotional weight.

Chbosky observes these seemingly small experiences with nuance and warmth. Charlie goes to football games, participates in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, reads books, makes mixtapes, spends time with Patrick and Sam, and tries to understand the unwritten social rules operating around him. Ultimately, the book prioritizes character growth and everyday moments over a grand, plot-driven climax.

9
'Stoner' (1965)

Image via Viking Press

"William Stoner entered the University of Missouri as a freshman in the year 1910, at the age of nineteen." The entire premise of Stoner could almost be summarized as "a man lives his life." William Stoner grows up on a Missouri farm, attends university, discovers a love of literature, becomes an academic, marries, has a daughter, experiences professional conflicts, falls in love with another woman, grows older, and eventually dies. There are no extraordinary adventures waiting for him and no secret destiny to fulfill, yet the book still hits hard emotionally.

Stoner's marriage becomes painfully unhappy, his relationship with his daughter is damaged, university politics make his professional life unnecessarily difficult, and one of his few genuinely fulfilling relationships cannot last. None of these events would make newspaper headlines. To the person experiencing them, however, they are the big things. Not for nothing, this book influenced later writers like Ian McEwan and Bret Easton Ellis.

8
'Kitchen' (1988)

"The place I like best in this world is the kitchen." Grief can make ordinary places feel enormously important. In Banana Yoshimoto's Kitchen, Mikage Sakurai finds comfort in kitchens after the death of her grandmother leaves her effectively alone. The protagonist eventually moves in with her friend Yuichi Tanabe and his transgender mother, Eriko, forming an unconventional new household while attempting to rebuild her life.

However, rather than constructing an elaborate plot around Mikage's loss, Yoshimoto concentrates on the rhythms through which people continue living after something fundamental has disappeared. Food becomes particularly important here. Mikage cooks, eats, studies culinary arts, and sleeps beside refrigerators, finding security in flavor and routine. These seemingly mundane activities become ways to heal. In this regard, the book is deeply rooted in the traditional Japanese aesthetic of mono no aware, wistful awareness of the impermanence of all things.

7
'Convenience Store Woman' (2016)

"A convenience store is a world of sound." Most people probably wouldn't consider working at a convenience store a calling. Keiko Furukura does. She's a 36-year-old woman who has spent 18 years working part-time at a Smile Mart in Tokyo. Keiko has never felt particularly comfortable with society's expectations, but the convenience store provides something wonderfully understandable. Every action has a purpose, employees have scripts to follow, products belong in specific places, and the sounds of the store tell her exactly what needs to happen next.

Put simply, the store gives Keiko a coherent role in an unstable world. The novel finds both comedy and genuine fascination in the routines of this environment. It helps that the main character is so perceptive. Through the glass windows of the Smile Mart, Keiko observes the changing seasons, the shifting habits of Tokyo workers, and the hidden details of the customers' lives.

6
'The Remains of the Day' (1989)

"It seems increasingly likely that I really will undertake the expedition that has been preoccupying my imagination now for some days." This was one of the early gems by Kazuo Ishiguro. In it, Stevens, an aging English butler, takes a trip through the countryside to visit former housekeeper Miss Kenton. Along the way, he remembers his decades of service at Darlington Hall, reflecting on his employer, his profession, his relationship with Miss Kenton, and his own commitment to the ideal of "dignity."

Gradually, however, those polite recollections reveal the enormous emotional consequences of a life spent suppressing almost everything personal. Stevens is a perfect slice-of-life protagonist because routine is effectively his worldview. Likewise, the heart of the book is found in quiet interactions: brief conversations in hallways, shared evening cocoa, and years of wordless glances between Stevens and Miss Kenton. It's in such moments that life can pass us by.

5
'Gilead' (2004)

"I told you last night that I might be gone sometime." In 1956, Reverend John Ames learns that his heart is failing and begins recording his thoughts for his seven-year-old son. What emerges isn't a conventional autobiography but something more intimate and wandering: memories, family history, theological reflections, observations about everyday life, and thoughts Ames hopes might someday allow his child to know the father he lost. The writing is unhurried, often stream-of-consciousness.

This is a book that very much believes in the power of paying attention to the world. Ames watches sunlight and observes his wife and son. He considers his own frailty and thinks back to experiences with his father and grandfather. The protagonist's faith informs practically everything he sees, but Gilead is less interested in preaching than in how sustained attention can make ordinary existence appear extraordinary. The novel was widely acclaimed, taking home several awards and making plenty of 'greatest novels' lists.

4
'My Struggle' (2009)

Image via Penguin Random House

"For the heart, life is simple: it beats for as long as it can." The Daniels' Everything Everywhere All at Once is one of the most maximalist films ever made: action comedy, multiverse sci-fi, family drama, existential crisis, and a genuinely earned emotional core that sneaks up on you amid the chaos. You are someone who responds to ambition, who doesn't want cinema to choose between being entertaining and being meaningful. This film refuses that choice entirely. It is overwhelming by design, and its overwhelming nature is precisely the point — because the feeling of being crushed by infinite possibility is exactly what it's about.
Oppenheimer

You are drawn to cinema on a grand scale — films that understand history not as a backdrop but as a force, and that place their characters inside that force and watch what happens. Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is a film about the terrifying gap between what we can do and what we should do, told with the full weight of one of the most consequential moments in human history behind it. You want your films to feel important without feeling self-important — to earn their ambition through sheer craft and the gravity of their subject. Oppenheimer does exactly that. It is enormous, complicated, and refuses easy comfort.
Birdman

You are drawn to films that foreground their own construction — that make the how of the filmmaking part of the what it's about. Alejandro González Iñárritu's Birdman, shot to appear as a single continuous take, is cinema examining itself through the cracked mirror of a fading actor's ego. You respond to formal daring, to the feeling that a film is doing something that probably shouldn't be possible. Michael Keaton's performance and Emmanuel Lubezki's restless camera create something genuinely unlike anything else — a film that is simultaneously about creativity, relevance, self-destruction, and the impossibility of ever truly knowing if your work means anything at all.

You are drawn to cinema that trusts silence, that refuses to explain itself, and that treats dread as a form of meaning. The Coen Brothers' No Country for Old Men is a film about the arrival of a new kind of evil — implacable, arbitrary, and utterly indifferent to the moral frameworks we use to make sense of the world. It is one of the most formally controlled films ever made, and its controlled restraint is what makes it so terrifying. You want your films to haunt you, not comfort you. You are not interested in resolution if resolution would be dishonest. No Country for Old Men is honest in a way that most cinema never dares to be.

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

While Naughty Dog has been busy working on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet for the last few years, fans have been wondering what comes next. With a stellar back catalog of gaming IP including the Uncharted franchise and The Last of Us duology, Naughty Dog has become legendary for creating and maintaining successful franchises. But with Uncharted 4: A Thief's End feeling like the finale for Nathan Drake's adventures, are we really getting an Uncharted 5 game soon?

Thanks to a message from NateTheHate over on X, we've learned that Shaun Escayg has been working on a secret project for almost three years. Shaun was a previous employee at Naughty Dog and helped with work on both Uncharted 4: A Thief's End and Uncharted: The Lost Legacy. WIth NateTheHate confirming that Shaun's next game isn't an installment of The Last of Us, it seems fairly likely that we're getting Uncharted 5 next.

Of course, it is possible that Shaun Escayg is working on a brand-new IP, but it seems less likely given his experience with the Uncharted franchise and the fact that launching a new IP is risky. With Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet being a new IP itself, it's very unlikely that Naughty Dog would follow it up with yet another new IP. The risk is simply too great and sticking to an already successful franchise is a much safer bet. All signs point to a new Uncharted game, but official confirmation has yet to surface.

The only other information we have about Shaun's secret project is a photo he shared himself on Instagram. It was a photo of a cannon taken in Trinidad & Tobago, and he captioned it as research for his upcoming game. So, if we're really getting a new Uncharted game, it seems likely that the setting might be in Trinidad. WIll we see further adventures of Nathan globe-trotting for one last time before retirement? Or perhaps his daughter Cassie has taken up the mantle and has an itchy trigger finger for pirates.

Paul Farrelly

WIth a full reveal for Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet set for 2027, it could be quite a while before we see any more details for Uncharted 5. Whether the game will be a prequel, sequel or franchise reboot remains to be seen, but Naughty Dog has done a stellar job of introducing gamers to a cast of characters with depth that could easily helm the franchise for future installments. A Sully and Sam team up could work well or perhaps even another adventure with Chloe and Nadine from Uncharted: The Lost Legacy.

Whatever happens next for the franchise is still unclear, but we're just happy to be getting Uncharted 5. Shaun Escayg and team certainly have the talents to deliver a 10/10 action adventure for gamers and once the dust settles on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, hopefully it will be all systems go on the next chapter of the Uncharted franchise. Uncharted 4: A Thief's End sets a high bar, but Naughty Dog has the chops to deliver yet another knockout epic adventure. Now when exactly is the next The Last of Us game coming out? items.title: Deadlock's gigantic new update gives its city a spooky new coat of paint and debuts 6 new heroes, including the one and only Rat King
items.author: Tyler Colp
items.summary: The cursed city where Deadlock's battles take place just got even spookier than it already was in the City Never Sleeps update. Valve's second major overhaul
items.text:
The cursed city where Deadlock's battles take place just got even spookier than it already was in the City Never Sleeps update. Valve's second major overhaul for the invite-only MOBA marks another major step in its pseudo-early access development, giving it a much stronger visual identity than it had before, six striking new heroes, and a massive list of tweaks to how it plays.

Deadlock's entire map has been redecorated into three distinct themes: a bright city center, a haunted university, and a shadowy stock exchange. All the buildings and creeps that inhabit each street have been redesigned to fit in. There are pickle jars with hands growing out of them lurking in the heart of the map, sentient stacks of books in the right lane, and slimy trashbag monsters in the left lane.

Squeezed between it all are four districts with their own identities, like a theater district infested with literal stage hands pulling the strings on steampunk-style automatons. Atop the Chinatown district is a bell tower where teams can fight over a fountain of souls to try to get a currency advantage in a tight match. Even the wooden crates that players smash for resources are now padlocked and bolted shut.

It's a whole new playground that will take some time for players to fully figure out. In the meantime, Valve has prepared six new heroes who will be released based on a player voting system, just like the previous set. My money's on the Rat King taking the lead because, well, he's the Rat King, a crowned rodent that began as a fan concept a year ago and quickly became a meme in the community.

Don't get me wrong, though, the others look great, too. Valve made a nurse who holds a needle like a gun, a Chess master who seems to float like Overwatch's Zenyatta, a skeleton who found a rocket launcher, a cozy old witch who I do not trust, and a young artist who wields a paintbrush. Two heroes will drop each week with the first making their debut on Friday.

(Image credit: Valve)Here's some other big changes I see on the update page:

Player health bars are bolder and more readable than before

There are now small indicators to help you see where nearby teammates are

The kill feed is considerably more clear when it comes to seeing who took out who

The entire shop interface is way more intuitive and includes filters for finding what you need fast

There are several new ways to ping locations and objects on the map

Characters have double the amount of voice lines as before and you can listen to them in a new menu

New tools let you create bots to practice on and there's a more comprehensive breakdown of combat details for the nerds out there

There are new accessibility options, like custom UI colors, subtitles, and options to automatically move, mantle, and shoot

All of this is only a fraction of the things Valve has added to the game, some of which it's intentionally keeping a secret so players can discover them on their own. Despite the size of the update, Valve hasn't removed the need for an invite to play Deadlock. One has to wonder how many of these it will take before the game is finally released to the public so everyone can get a taste of what Valve's been cooking up.

items.title: Ace Combat 8 Steam reviewers are steaming mad about its pre-order bonus not being a standalone app
items.author: wesley@pcgamer.com (Wes Fenlon)
items.summary: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is technically out on Thursday, but as is commonplace now folks who pre-order the $90 deluxe edition get to hop into the cockpit
items.text:
Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is technically out on Thursday, but as is commonplace now folks who pre-order the $90 deluxe edition get to hop into the cockpit a few days early. Anyone who pre-orders the $70 standard edition, meanwhile, gets a pretty sweet bonus: Ace Combat Zero, a 2006 entry in the series that has never been on PC before now. But how Bandai Namco has packaged Zero is now threatening to drag the new game's Steam review average down into Mixed territory.

Of the nearly 1,000 negative reviews as of this writing, there's a spread of complaints—performance, multiplayer connectivity, weightier flight physics, lacking HOTAS support—but one of the most common refrains is that the Zero bonus has been something of a bait-and-switch. As summarized by reviewer Akion:

"Before I bought the game the description said this about the Belkan War DLC Half the reason I got the game was because that is my all time fav. The integrity of this should matter to you.

"'*ACE COMBAT ZERO: THE BELKAN WAR is a standalone application separate from the ACE COMBAT 8: WINGS OF THEVE full game.'

"And now it says this:

"*ACE COMBAT ZERO: THE BELKAN WAR (Steam Version) is available as a DLC executable launched separately from the base game."

So why does this matter?

As another reviewer points out, "You need to install 140gb of data to play a 3gb 20 years old game." That's not an exaggeration: Ace Combat 8 is currently using up 140.24 gigs on my SSD, with the Zero DLC making up only 3.2GB of that total.

There's also a clear strain of dissatisfaction with the fact that on consoles, Zero comes along with its own achievements/trophies list, which is absent for the Steam version. Since it's tied to AC8, Zero also lacks separate cloud saves, something that would be pretty nice for playing it on the Steam Deck, where it should run very well given its age.

The lack of parity with the console version clearly has quite a few players annoyed, but the principle of the thing seems to be the biggest sticking point. The store page said Zero would be a separate app, and then it wasn't.

Some folks have countered that Bandai Namco couldn't release Zero as its own package due to the licensing terms of the planes featured in the game, seemingly based on this livestream featuring the developers on September 28 saying the licenses only permit giving the game away for free. But clearly it's possible to package the game separately on consoles even without selling it, and I'm skeptical it's impossible to find some kind of workaround on Steam. Hitman 3 still has a listing page, for example, despite not being purchasable by itself—it's listed as downloadable content for Hitman World of Assassination.

"Notice: At the request of the publisher, HITMAN 3 Access Pass: HITMAN 1 Complete First Season is unlisted on the Steam store and will not appear in search," reads a warning message at the top of the store page.

This criticism will soon show up in a smaller portion of Ace Combat 8's reviews as players who didn't bother to pre-order begin to filter into the reaction pool, but for now the pre-order bonus isn't quite the clean publicity win it otherwise could've been.

items.text:
Japan’s Smallest and Least-Populated Major Island Is a World of Pilgrimages, Delicious Food and Plenty of Forest Bathing

Each year, more than 100,000 people hike at least part of a 750-mile route on Shikoku that connects 88 Buddhist temples and other sacred sites

Laura Kiniry
| Travel Correspondent

September 29, 2026 3:40 p.m.

I had just arrived at Konsen-ji, the third temple on Japan’s Shikoku Pilgrimage route, when a young Japanese girl presented me with two origami cranes. These tiny gifts, I would later learn, symbolized wishes for a safe and smooth journey along the 750-mile circuit connecting 88 Buddhist temples, as well as other sacred sites, on Shikoku, the smallest and least populated of Japan’s four main islands.

On my week-long visit to Shikoku, I encountered many acts of kindness, from the innkeeper at Sudachi-an, a local guesthouse in the village of Nabeiwa, driving me to my lodging when I ended up lost in the rain, to a taxi driver insisting that I take a couple of sweet, kiyomi oranges to help sustain me on my day’s trek. This rural Japanese island is a place where history, hospitality and natural beauty converge.

The 7,063-square-mile island is the most rustic and remote. In fact, the first bridge connecting Shikoku to the main island of Honshu, where you’ll find big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto, wasn’t built until 1988. Even today, only three routes connect the two islands. Shikoku is a quiet rural slice of Japan where Westerners remain a rarity, though that’s slowly changing.

The Shikoku Pilgrimage is one of the island’s top draws for travelers. Between 100,000 and 150,000 people undertake at least part of the route annually, with the best times of year for walking the circular trail being spring and fall. All its sites are associated with Kobo Daishi, a Japanese monk who lived during the ninth century and founded Shingon, a major school of Buddhism that focuses on the attainment of enlightenment during a practitioner’s lifetime. While the individual temples and sacred sites span a variety of dates, mostly from the eighth century onward, the circuit itself wasn’t fully established until the late 16th to early 17th century. About 80 percent of the route is paved asphalt and concrete, often passing through small towns and farmlands. However, the rest of the pathway winds along dirt trails and ascends steep mountainsides and ancient stone steps through sections of remote wilderness. Along the way, pilgrims tend to stay in a mix of traditional ryokan (Japanese-style hotels), shukubo (temple stays) and local family inns. Most provide food, and some have onsens for bathing. Pilgrims are considered the manifestation of Kobo Daishi. “So when people are helping you, they’re actually helping him directly.”

According to Moreton, this notion has led to a culture of hospitality that has spread throughout the island. He says it’s this feeling of welcomeness that draws people to the island and persuades them to return to the pilgrimage.

Bennett, for example, has completed the route four times. “There’s a word for people like me,” he says. “Shikoku-byo. It means ‘Shikoku sickness.’” He says that people are drawn to the circuit again and again both for the inner peace it offers and the kindness of Shikoku’s residents. “I would just catch ‘the sickness’ and want to return.” So ten years ago, he moved to Japan from the United States.

The Japanese word Shikoku means “four countries.” It’s an accurate description, since the island is broken up into four prefectures: Ehime, Kagawa, Kochi and Tokushima. Geographically, they’re separated by the Shikoku Mountains, creating four distinct regions, each with its own unique culture and cuisine. However, the Shikoku Pilgrimage route connects them all.

“Each prefecture on the island is different,” says Moreton, “in the same way that the U.S. South is very different from California and New York.”

The sparsely populated Kochi Prefecture on the island’s south side is a natural food capital, with fruits like juicy musk melon, caramelly sweet Niitaka pears, and, most famously, tart yuzu. At Umaji Onsen, guests can soak in yuzu baths during winter solstice and dine on inaka sushi—a local delicacy made with mountain vegetables instead of fish, and yuzu-infused sticky rice.

Kagawa Prefecture is famously known as the “Udon Prefecture.” In the historic town of Kotohira, the Nakano Udon School invites visitors to “dance” on dough, stomping on it with their feet to create the noodle’s chewy texture. Ehime Prefecture is brimming with natural scenery and hot springs, including the famous Dogo Onsen—inspiration for the bathhouse in the 2002 animated film Spirited Away. Tokushima Prefecture (nearest to Honshu) produces the vast majority of Japan’s natural indigo dye. Naruto, a city in Tokushima, is also home to Otani Ware, a traditional Japanese pottery known for its iron-rich clay and an unusual “lying down” wheel technique. The enormous rustic earthenware jars are used to ferment indigo leaves. The pottery’s origins are also directly connected to the Shikoku Pilgrimage: Bun’emon, the Japanese craftsman who brought the pottery wheel to Tokushima in the late-18th century, had first come to Shikoku to visit its 88 sacred sites.

“There’s so much interesting history and culture related to the pilgrimage across Shikoku,” says Moreton. In addition to Otani Ware, he tells me about the World War I era Bando Prisoner of War Camp in Naruto. I passed the site commemorating it on my walk to Ryozenji, the first temple on the pilgrimage. Known as German Village Park, it marks the camp where the Japanese held approximately 1,000 German soldiers, who were given surprisingly free rein. “Tokushima has always had that open feeling to outsiders,” Moreton says, thanks to the community’s deep-rooted tradition of o-settai. Residents received them openly and showed humane kindness, and the Germans taught locals how to play orchestral instruments, make beer and bake German-style bread, which some Naruto bakeries still sell today.

By the end of my week on Shikoku I had hiked nearly 30 miles up severely steep inclines and through forests popping with spring flowers, sat beside koi-filled ponds and followed statues of the beloved Bodhisattva Jizō—the guardian of travelers—often with nobody else in sight for miles at a time. But it was those moments when I did encounter others, whether it was my orange-giving taxi driver or fellow pilgrims on the trail, and the hospitality they showed this solo traveler that have stuck with me most.

After all, Shikoku has welcomed pilgrims for hundreds of years.
